---
title: "Prediction and Bayesian model averaging"
subtitle: "Lecture 9"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can turn a posterior into a forecast that is honest
about two separate kinds of ignorance, not knowing the parameters of a model and not
knowing which model deserves to be trusted, and average across candidates rather than
betting everything on the one that fits best today.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

With $J$ candidate models, each with its own parameters and its own likelihood, Bayes'
theorem applied to the model index itself gives a posterior probability for each
model, $p(M_j \mid y) \propto p(y \mid M_j)\,p(M_j)$, and the forecast that reflects
every candidate at once is the model-averaged posterior predictive,

$$
p(y^\ast \mid y) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} p(M_j \mid y)\; p\big(y^\ast \mid y, M_j\big).
$$

This mixes each model's own forecast distribution in proportion to how well it has
already explained the data, rather than discarding every candidate but one. Its
difficulty is that the number of candidates grows exponentially in the number of
things one is unsure about, and the weight attached to each candidate is itself
estimated with error that a forecaster who reports only the leading model never has to
confront.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. derive the posterior predictive distribution of the Normal linear model and show
   why it is wider than a forecast that plugs in the posterior mean;
2. diagnose why selecting the single best-fitting model overstates how much that
   model should be trusted out of sample;
3. derive the model-averaged predictive distribution and the sense in which the
   marginal likelihood already penalises an unnecessarily large model;
4. implement Bayesian model averaging over a set of candidate return predictors and
   grade its forecasts with the log predictive score;
5. compare model averaging against model selection, a maximal model and a
   no-predictability benchmark in an expanding-window backtest;
6. interpret a predictive density's calibration as a question distinct from whether
   its centre carries any information at all.

Week 9 of 15, paired with the [Week 9 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/09-prediction-bma.qmd). The chapter assumes the
Normal-Inverse-Gamma regression posterior of Lecture 2; the state-space filtering of
Lecture 8 is not needed, because every candidate model considered here has fixed
coefficients.

## Motivation: the best model in sample is not the best model out of sample {#sec-motivation}

Every model comparison since Lecture 6 has used the data to say which specification
fits best, and it has been natural to read that as saying which specification to
trust going forward. Whether that reading survives contact with data is itself a
testable question, and predicting the market's own return is the sharpest place to
ask it, because the return-predictability literature has spent forty years arguing
about a handful of candidate predictors without settling on one.

We take five variables the literature has used to predict the market's monthly excess
return, the term spread, the change in the federal funds rate, inflation, unemployment
and last month's return, giving $2^5 = 32$ candidate models once the constant-only
model and every subset of predictors are included. Fitting all thirty-two on data
through December 1994 and ranking them by marginal likelihood identifies a single
best-supported specification. The question is whether that specification goes on to
forecast well over the following three decades, which nothing so far in the course has
had to check, because every previous chapter's model comparisons ended at the fitted
sample.

**Reading the computation.** Every model is fit once on the training months and then
scored, unchanged, against every remaining month; nothing about the test period
enters the fit. `fit_g` and its helper functions are the same ones defined in full in
@sec-empirical and are used here in their simplest form, evidence on a fixed sample.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
from itertools import combinations
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.special import gammaln, logsumexp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
fred_p = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet")
ff_p = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
cpi_yoy = 100.0 * np.log(fred_p["cpi"]).diff(12)

panel = pd.DataFrame({
    "term_spread": fred_p["yield_10y"] - fred_p["fed_funds"],
    "d_ffr": fred_p["fed_funds"].diff(),
    "inflation": cpi_yoy.shift(1),
    "unemp": fred_p["unemployment"].shift(1),
    "lag_ret": 100.0 * ff_p["mkt_rf"],
})
panel["target"] = 100.0 * ff_p["mkt_rf"].shift(-1)
panel = panel.dropna()
pred_names = ["term_spread", "d_ffr", "inflation", "unemp", "lag_ret"]
Zp, yp = panel[pred_names].to_numpy(), panel["target"].to_numpy()
n_p, k_p = Zp.shape
dates_p = panel.index
a0, d0 = 2.5, 2.5

def nig_posterior(X, y, b0, V0, a0, d0):
    V0_inv = np.linalg.inv(V0)
    V_bar = np.linalg.inv(V0_inv + X.T @ X)
    b_bar = V_bar @ (V0_inv @ b0 + X.T @ y)
    Q = (y - X @ b_bar) @ y + (b0 - b_bar) @ V0_inv @ b0
    return b_bar, V_bar, a0 + 0.5 * y.size, d0 + 0.5 * Q

def predictive_t(x_star, b_bar, V_bar, a_bar, d_bar):
    return 2 * a_bar, x_star @ b_bar, np.sqrt(d_bar / a_bar * (1 + x_star @ V_bar @ x_star))

def log_marglik(X, y, b0, V0, a0, d0):
    b_bar, V_bar, a_bar, d_bar = nig_posterior(X, y, b0, V0, a0, d0)
    ld0, ldb = np.linalg.slogdet(V0)[1], np.linalg.slogdet(V_bar)[1]
    return (-0.5 * y.size * np.log(2 * np.pi) + 0.5 * (ldb - ld0)
            + gammaln(a_bar) - gammaln(a0) + a0 * np.log(d0) - a_bar * np.log(d_bar))

def gprior(X, g):
    return np.zeros(X.shape[1]), g * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)

models_r = [tuple(s) for kk in range(k_p + 1) for s in combinations(range(k_p), kk)]
labels_r = ["{" + ", ".join(pred_names[j] for j in m) + "}" if m else "{constant only}"
            for m in models_r]

def fit_g(rows):
    g = float(len(rows))
    lml = np.empty(len(models_r))
    for j, m in enumerate(models_r):
        Xm = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(rows))] + [Zp[rows, i] for i in m])
        b0m, V0m = gprior(Xm, g)
        lml[j] = log_marglik(Xm, yp[rows], b0m, V0m, a0, d0)
    return lml

t_split = dates_p.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("1994-12-01"))
train, test = np.arange(t_split + 1), np.arange(t_split + 1, n_p)
lml_tr = fit_g(train)
j_train, j_const = np.argmax(lml_tr), models_r.index(())

oos_scores = np.empty(len(models_r))
for j, m in enumerate(models_r):
    Xtr = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(train))] + [Zp[train, i] for i in m])
    b0m, V0m = gprior(Xtr, float(len(train)))
    post = nig_posterior(Xtr, yp[train], b0m, V0m, a0, d0)
    Xte = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(test))] + [Zp[test, i] for i in m])
    oos_scores[j] = np.mean([stats.t.logpdf(yp[test[i]], *predictive_t(Xte[i], *post))
                             for i in range(len(test))])
j_oos = np.argmax(oos_scores)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
ax.scatter(lml_tr, oos_scores, color="grey", alpha=0.6, s=28)
ax.scatter(lml_tr[j_train], oos_scores[j_train], color="C3", s=90, zorder=5,
           label=f"best in-sample: {labels_r[j_train]}")
ax.scatter(lml_tr[j_oos], oos_scores[j_oos], color="C2", s=90, zorder=5,
           label=f"best out-of-sample: {labels_r[j_oos]}")
ax.scatter(lml_tr[j_const], oos_scores[j_const], color="C7", s=90, zorder=5,
           label="constant only")
ax.set_xlabel("in-sample log marginal likelihood (through 1994)")
ax.set_ylabel("mean out-of-sample log predictive score (1995-2026)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Thirty-two models: fit through 1994 against performance after it")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"training sample: {len(train)} months through {dates_p[t_split]:%Y-%m}; "
      f"test sample: {len(test)} months to {dates_p[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"best in-sample model: {labels_r[j_train]}, log ML {lml_tr[j_train]:.2f}")
print(f"its out-of-sample rank among the 32 candidates: "
      f"{int((oos_scores > oos_scores[j_train]).sum()) + 1}")
print(f"its out-of-sample score {oos_scores[j_train]:.4f} against the constant-only "
      f"model's {oos_scores[j_const]:.4f}")
print(f"correlation of in-sample log ML with out-of-sample score across the 32 models: "
      f"{np.corrcoef(lml_tr, oos_scores)[0,1]:.3f}")
```

The picture has no visible upward slope, and the number confirms it: across the
thirty-two candidates, in-sample fit and subsequent performance correlate at
$-0.073$, indistinguishable from zero and if anything the wrong sign. The model that
looked best through 1994, the one built on the term spread alone, ranks twenty-fourth
of thirty-two once graded on the following three decades, and its out-of-sample score
of $-2.9317$ is worse than the constant-only model's $-2.9265$: a researcher in 1994
who selected the best-fitting specification and used it for the next thirty years
would have done worse than one who used no predictors at all. Choosing the single
model that best explains the past is not obviously choosing the model that best
anticipates the future, and the rest of this chapter is about why, and what to do
instead.

## The problem: a model chosen by its own fit overstates that fit {#sec-problem}

### Result R-9.1: selecting the best of many candidates is a biased estimate of its own quality

Let $X_1, \dots, X_J$ be the in-sample fit statistics, for instance the log marginal
likelihoods above, that a set of $J$ candidate models would earn on hypothetical
repetitions of the same sampling process, each with some finite mean $\mathbb
E[X_j]$. Then

$$
\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j} X_j\Big] \;\ge\; \max_{j}\, \mathbb E[X_j],
$$

for any $J \ge 1$ and any joint distribution of the $X_j$ with finite means, with
equality only in the degenerate case where one model dominates every replication or
all the $X_j$ are almost surely equal to their means. The gap on the left is what a
researcher who selects the best-fitting model and reports its own fit statistic as
evidence of quality is quoting; the right-hand side is the truth for whichever model
happens to be best on average. Selecting by fit and then citing that fit is therefore
optimistic in expectation, the more so the more candidates are compared and the
noisier each one's fit statistic is.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The function $x \mapsto \max_j x_j$ on $\mathbb R^J$ is convex: it is the pointwise
maximum of the $J$ coordinate projections, each of which is linear and therefore
convex, and a pointwise maximum of convex functions is convex. Jensen's inequality
states that for any convex function $g$ and any random vector $X$ with finite mean,
$\mathbb E[g(X)] \ge g(\mathbb E[X])$. Applying it with $g(x) = \max_j x_j$ and
$X = (X_1,\dots,X_J)$ gives immediately

$$
\mathbb E\Big[\max_j X_j\Big] \ge \max_j \mathbb E[X_j],
$$

which is the displayed result; no assumption beyond finite means and the definition of
the maximum was used, so it holds for any $J$, any correlation structure among the
$X_j$, and any sample size behind each one.

Equality in Jensen's inequality for a strictly convex function on a set of positive
measure requires the random vector to be almost surely constant along the direction
that matters, here that the identity of the maximising coordinate never changes across
replications and its value never varies either; short of that degenerate case the
inequality is strict. The gap grows with $J$ because adding another candidate can only
weakly increase $\max_j X_j$ in every replication while leaving $\max_j \mathbb E[X_j]$
unchanged unless the newcomer is the new true best, and it grows with the variance of
each $X_j$ because a noisier fit statistic gives the maximum more room to be pulled up
by chance in some replications without a compensating pull down, since the maximum can
never fall below what any single candidate achieves. This is the same arithmetic
familiar from extreme value theory and from the winner's curse in auctions: the
winning bid is a biased estimate of the value of what was won, for exactly the reason
that it was selected for being the largest number in the room.
:::

The inequality can be checked directly rather than taken on faith, by resampling the
training period many times and comparing the average of the best fit found each time
against the best of the average fits.

**Reading the computation.** Each replication resamples the training months in blocks
of a year, preserving some of the short-run dependence in monthly returns, and refits
all thirty-two models. The two quantities compared are not the same object: one
averages after taking the maximum, the other takes the maximum after averaging.

```{python}
#| label: fig-jensen-check
#| fig-cap: "Distribution, across 300 resamples of the training period, of the best log marginal likelihood found in that resample. The vertical line is the best model's average log marginal likelihood across the same resamples."
boot_rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n_boot, block = 300, 12
n_blocks = int(np.ceil(len(train) / block))
lml_boot = np.empty((n_boot, len(models_r)))
for b in range(n_boot):
    starts = boot_rng.integers(0, len(train) - block, size=n_blocks)
    idx = np.concatenate([train[s:s + block] for s in starts])[:len(train)]
    lml_boot[b] = fit_g(idx)

mean_of_max = lml_boot.max(axis=1).mean()
max_of_mean = lml_boot.mean(axis=0).max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
ax.hist(lml_boot.max(axis=1), bins=30, color="C0", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(max_of_mean, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5,
           label=r"$\max_j \mathbb{E}[X_j]$ (estimated)")
ax.axvline(mean_of_max, color="C3", lw=1.5,
           label=r"$\mathbb{E}[\max_j X_j]$ (estimated)")
ax.set_xlabel("best log marginal likelihood in a resample")
ax.set_ylabel("count")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("The average of the best is not the best of the average")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"E[max_j X_j] (estimated by resampling) = {mean_of_max:.3f}")
print(f"max_j E[X_j] (estimated by resampling)  = {max_of_mean:.3f}")
print(f"estimated gap = {mean_of_max - max_of_mean:.3f} log points")
```

The gap is $1.496$ log points, positive as R-9.1 requires, and it is not a small
number on the scale these models are compared: @sec-empirical below finds a log Bayes
factor of only $0.02$ separating the best and second-best specifications on the full
sample, so an optimism bias of this size is easily large enough to decide which
model looks best even when the true difference between candidates is close to
nothing. Whatever fit statistic is used to pick a winner among many candidates, part of
that winner's apparent advantage is the advantage of having been chosen out of many,
not the advantage of being correct, and R-9.1 says this is true before any data are
even examined, purely as a consequence of taking a maximum over more than one
candidate.

## Methodology: averaging over parameters, then over models {#sec-methodology}

Two separate kinds of not-knowing are in play, and the repair handles them in two
layers. Within a single model, the parameters $\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ are unknown and
a forecast should integrate over them rather than plugging in a point estimate.
Across models, which specification is correct is itself unknown, and a forecast
should integrate over that too, exactly as R-9.1 says a forecaster who instead
commits to one specification is trusting a number more than the evidence supports.

### Result R-9.2: the posterior predictive distribution is a Student t, wider than the plug-in forecast

Let $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_n)$, with the natural
conjugate prior $\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim N(b_0, \sigma^2 V_0)$ and $\sigma^2 \sim
IG(a_0,d_0)$, so the posterior is again Normal-Inverse-Gamma with moments $\bar V =
(V_0^{-1}+X^\top X)^{-1}$, $\bar b = \bar V(V_0^{-1}b_0 + X^\top y)$, $\bar a =
a_0+n/2$ and $\bar d = d_0 + \tfrac12\big[(y-X\bar b)^\top y + (b_0-\bar
b)^\top V_0^{-1}b_0\big]$. For a future observation $y^\ast$ with known row $x_\ast$,

$$
y^\ast \mid y \;\sim\; t_{2\bar a}\!\left(x_\ast^\top \bar b,\;\;
\frac{\bar d}{\bar a}\big(1 + x_\ast^\top \bar V x_\ast\big)\right),
$$

for any $n$, any number of regressors $k$ and any $x_\ast$. The plug-in forecast fixes
the parameters at their posterior means and reports $N(x_\ast^\top\bar b,
\hat\sigma^2)$: the same centre, but missing both the extra term $x_\ast^\top \bar
Vx_\ast$, coefficient uncertainty that grows as $x_\ast$ moves away from where the data
were observed, and the heavier tails that come from not knowing $\sigma^2$ exactly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Integrate in two stages, first over $\beta$ at fixed $\sigma^2$, then over $\sigma^2$.
At fixed $\sigma^2$, $y^\ast = x_\ast^\top\beta + \varepsilon^\ast$ is an affine function
of the Normal $\beta \mid \sigma^2, y \sim N(\bar b, \sigma^2\bar V)$ plus an
independent $N(0,\sigma^2)$ shock, hence Normal with mean $x_\ast^\top\bar b$ and
variance $\sigma^2 c$, $c \equiv 1 + x_\ast^\top\bar Vx_\ast$, the leading one being the
future shock's own variance and the second term the coefficient uncertainty carried
through $x_\ast$. Writing $r = (y^\ast - x_\ast^\top\bar b)^2$, the second stage
integrates this Normal density against the Inverse-Gamma density of $\sigma^2$,

$$
p(y^\ast \mid y) \propto \int_0^\infty (\sigma^2)^{-\bar a - 3/2}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\Big[\bar d + \frac{r}{2c}\Big]\right) d\sigma^2,
$$

after collecting the two exponentials and the powers of $\sigma^2$. The integrand is an
unnormalised $IG(\bar a + \tfrac12, \bar d + r/(2c))$ kernel, so the integral is the
reciprocal of that density's normalising constant, giving $p(y^\ast\mid y) \propto
\big(1 + r/(2c\bar a\,\bar d/\bar a)\big)^{-\bar a - 1/2}$ after factoring $\bar d$ out
of the bracket. Matching this shape against the Student $t$ density, proportional to
$(1+(y-\mu)^2/(\nu s^2))^{-(\nu+1)/2}$, gives $\nu = 2\bar a$ and $s^2 = c\bar d/\bar
a$, the displayed result.

Two features of this shape matter beyond the algebra. The degrees of freedom $2\bar a
= 2a_0+n$ grow with the sample, so the $t$ converges to a Normal as $n\to\infty$: heavy
predictive tails are a small-sample consequence of not knowing $\sigma^2$ and vanish
once it is well pinned down. The factor $c = 1+x_\ast^\top\bar Vx_\ast$, by contrast,
never vanishes, because its leading term is the variance of a shock that has not
happened yet and no quantity of data removes it; a long sample shrinks the interval
around the conditional mean to nothing while the interval around a future realised
outcome converges to a fixed width set by $\sigma$, and confusing the two is a common
error in reporting a forecast interval.
:::

### Result R-9.3: model averaging as one more layer of the same integral, with an automatic penalty for size

With $J$ models each given a prior probability $p(M_j)$, Bayes' theorem applied to the
model index gives the posterior model probability

$$
p(M_j \mid y) \propto p(y \mid M_j)\,p(M_j), \qquad
p(y \mid M_j) = \iint p(y \mid \beta,\sigma^2,M_j)\,p(\beta,\sigma^2\mid M_j)\,
d\beta\,d\sigma^2,
$$

and the model-averaged predictive mixes each model's own R-9.2 distribution in
proportion to these weights, $p(y^\ast\mid y) = \sum_j p(M_j\mid y)\,p(y^\ast\mid
y,M_j)$. Because the chain rule factorises $p(y\mid M_j) = \prod_t p(y_t\mid
y_{1:t-1},M_j)$ with no assumption beyond the model already written down, the marginal
likelihood is literally a cumulative in-sample log predictive score, the same currency
used to grade a forecast out of sample. It also penalises size with no term added by
hand: a model that spreads its prior over a larger parameter space must divide its
prior density more thinly, and therefore assigns less of it to the one dataset
actually observed, unless the extra parameters earn their keep by improving the fit
enough to compensate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Write the natural conjugate marginal likelihood as $p(y\mid M) = (2\pi)^{-n/2}
|\bar V|^{1/2}|V_0|^{-1/2}\,\Gamma(\bar a)/\Gamma(a_0)\cdot d_0^{a_0}/\bar d^{\,\bar a}$,
so everything that depends on the size of the model rather than the fit sits in the
determinant ratio $|\bar V|/|V_0|$. Since $\bar V^{-1} = V_0^{-1} + X^\top X$ and
$X^\top X$ is positive semi-definite, $\bar V^{-1} \succeq V_0^{-1}$ in the Loewner
order, which implies $\bar V \preceq V_0$ in the same order and hence $|\bar V| \le
|V_0|$ for any design and any prior, with equality only when $X^\top X = 0$, that is,
when the regressors carry no information at all. The ratio $|\bar V|/|V_0| \in (0,1]$
is therefore always a genuine penalty, and it applies model by model regardless of
whether the extra columns of $X$ turn out to matter: enlarging a model by adding a
column to $X$ and a corresponding row and column to $V_0$ enlarges the space the prior
must cover before any data are seen, shrinking this ratio further unless the new
column is informative enough to shrink $|\bar V|$ by at least as much as $|V_0|$ grew.

The chain-rule factorisation of the marginal likelihood is exact for any joint density,
$p(y_{1:n}\mid M) = \prod_{t=1}^n p(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1}, M)$, so the log marginal
likelihood is $\sum_t \log p(y_t\mid y_{1:t-1},M)$, a sum of one-step-ahead log
predictive densities computed in exactly the sense R-9.2 defines them, using only data
up to $t-1$ at each term. Ranking models by marginal likelihood is therefore ranking
them by cumulative in-sample forecasting performance under the model's own prior, which
is the same object, on the same log scale, that an out-of-sample backtest reports; the
two can disagree, as @sec-motivation already showed they can, but they are commensurable
rather than being two different currencies.
:::

Averaging over models is not a hedge added on top of averaging over parameters; it is
the same operation, mixing over one more layer of what remains unknown, and R-9.1
says why skipping this layer and reporting the single best-supported model is
optimistic exactly to the degree that the comparison among candidates is close.

## Data: the market's excess return and five candidate predictors, 1961 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset, used in every section from here on and never swapped for
another, is the monthly Fama-French market excess return together with five variables
the return-predictability literature has proposed as predictors: the term spread, the
change in the federal funds rate, year-on-year consumer price inflation, the
unemployment rate, and the market's own lagged return. Timing is enforced explicitly:
the term spread and the funds-rate change are built from rates known within month
$t$, inflation and unemployment are lagged one further month to match their
publication schedule, and the target is next month's return, so every predictor used
to forecast month $t+1$ was public before that month began.

```{python}
#| label: fig-market-return-series
#| fig-cap: "The market's monthly excess return, 1961 to 2026, the chapter's single forecasting target."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.6))
ax.plot(dates_p, yp, color="steelblue", lw=0.5)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("market excess return (%)")
ax.set_title("The forecasting target: next month's market excess return")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{n_p} months, {dates_p[0]:%Y-%m} to {dates_p[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(panel.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3).T)
print("\ncorrelation of each predictor with next month's return:")
print(panel.corr()["target"][pred_names].round(4))
```

Seven hundred and eighty-four months of data give a market excess return averaging
$0.593$ percentage points a month with a standard deviation of $4.460$, an annualised
Sharpe ratio near $0.46$. Every predictor correlates with next month's return at
under one tenth in absolute value, with the signs the literature reports: the term
spread and unemployment positively, the funds-rate change and inflation negatively. A
correlation of $0.09$ implies an $R^2$ of about eight tenths of one percent from a
single regressor, and that number, not any failure of the data, is the whole reason
model uncertainty is severe here: with a signal this weak, thirty-two candidate
specifications are never going to be decisively separated by sixty-five years of
monthly observations.

## Empirical analysis: does averaging over the thirty-two models help? {#sec-empirical}

### Enumerating the models

With five predictors and an always-included intercept there are $2^5 = 32$ models, few
enough to enumerate exactly. Each gets Zellner's g-prior, $V_0 = g(X^\top X)^{-1}$
with the unit-information choice $g = n$, a standard convenient prior that scales
automatically with the units of each regressor; its properties are derived in the
supplementary material for the exercise session. `fit_full` below fits every model on
a set of rows and, when asked, scores one future observation.

**Reading the computation.** Posterior model probabilities are normalised in log space
with `logsumexp` because the individual marginal likelihoods are astronomically small
numbers whose ratios are all that matter.

```{python}
def fit_full(rows, x_row=None, y_new=None):
    g = float(len(rows))
    lml = np.empty(len(models_r)); ld = np.full(len(models_r), np.nan)
    mu = np.full(len(models_r), np.nan); sc = np.full(len(models_r), np.nan)
    nu = np.full(len(models_r), np.nan)
    for j, m in enumerate(models_r):
        Xm = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(rows))] + [Zp[rows, i] for i in m])
        b0m, V0m = gprior(Xm, g)
        lml[j] = log_marglik(Xm, yp[rows], b0m, V0m, a0, d0)
        if x_row is not None:
            post = nig_posterior(Xm, yp[rows], b0m, V0m, a0, d0)
            nu[j], mu[j], sc[j] = predictive_t(np.r_[1.0, x_row[list(m)]], *post)
            ld[j] = stats.t.logpdf(y_new, nu[j], mu[j], sc[j])
    return np.exp(lml - logsumexp(lml)), lml, ld, mu, sc, nu

w_r, lml_r, *_ = fit_full(np.arange(n_p))
j_const = models_r.index(())
j_full_r = models_r.index(tuple(range(k_p)))
pip_r = np.array([w_r[[j for j, m in enumerate(models_r) if v in m]].sum()
                  for v in range(k_p)])

print(f"posterior probability of the constant-only model: {w_r[j_const]:.4f}")
print(f"log Bayes factor, best model over constant only: {lml_r.max() - lml_r[j_const]:.2f}")
print(f"log Bayes factor, best model over the full model: {lml_r.max() - lml_r[j_full_r]:.2f}")
print("posterior inclusion probabilities:",
      {pred_names[v]: round(float(pip_r[v]), 3) for v in range(k_p)})
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-posterior-models
#| fig-cap: "Left: posterior probability of the six best-supported models, out of thirty-two, on the full sample. Right: posterior inclusion probability of each predictor against the prior line of one half."
ord_r = np.argsort(w_r)[::-1][:6]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
cols = ["C7" if j == j_const else "C0" for j in ord_r]
axes[0].bar(range(6), w_r[ord_r], color=cols,
            tick_label=[labels_r[j].replace(", ", ",\n") for j in ord_r])
axes[0].set_ylabel("posterior model probability"); axes[0].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
axes[0].set_title("Six best-supported models")
axes[1].bar(pred_names, pip_r, color="C2")
axes[1].axhline(0.5, color="grey", ls=":", label="prior inclusion probability")
axes[1].set_ylabel("posterior inclusion probability"); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); axes[1].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25, labelsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("Posterior inclusion probabilities")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Read on the whole sample, this is a negative result. The best-supported single model
contains only the funds-rate change, with posterior probability $0.1702$; the
second-best is the constant-only model at $0.1676$. The log Bayes factor of the best
model over the constant is $0.02$, not weak evidence but no evidence, and every
predictor's inclusion probability sits below the prior value of one half, meaning the
data have argued against every one of them individually even as the full model is
rejected by $7.81$ log points against the best single predictor. After sixty-five
years and five of the profession's favourite predictors, the evidence cannot separate
a world with predictable returns from one without.

### An expanding-window backtest from 1990

**Reading the computation.** At every month from January 1990 the model set is refit
on data available up to but not including that month, so nothing after month $t$
enters the forecast issued for month $t$. BMA scores the probability-weighted mixture;
selection scores whichever model has the highest posterior probability that month;
full always uses all five predictors; the benchmark is the constant-only model.

```{python}
t_start = dates_p.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("1990-01-01"))
rec = []
for t in range(t_start, n_p):
    w, lml, ld, mu, sc, nu = fit_full(np.arange(t), Zp[t], yp[t])
    jb = int(np.argmax(w))
    rec.append({"date": dates_p[t], "y": yp[t], "top_w": w.max(),
                "lps_bma": logsumexp(ld + np.log(w)), "lps_sel": ld[jb],
                "lps_full": ld[j_full_r], "lps_bench": ld[j_const],
                "mu_bma": float(w @ mu), "mu_bench": mu[j_const]})
bt = pd.DataFrame(rec).set_index("date")

def r2_oos(mu_col):
    e = bt["y"] - bt[mu_col]; base = bt["y"] - bt["mu_bench"]
    return 1.0 - (e @ e) / (base @ base)

strategies = [("BMA", "bma"), ("best single model", "sel"),
              ("full model", "full"), ("prevailing mean", "bench")]
print(f"{len(bt)} out-of-sample months, {bt.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {bt.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(pd.DataFrame({"mean log score": [bt["lps_"+s].mean() for _, s in strategies],
                    "cumulative log score": [bt["lps_"+s].sum() for _, s in strategies]},
                   index=[nm for nm, _ in strategies]).round(4))
print(f"\nmean weight on the leading model: {bt['top_w'].mean():.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-backtest-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative log score minus the prevailing-mean benchmark, 1990 to 2026, for BMA, model selection and the full model."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.2))
for lab, key, col in [("BMA", "bma", "C0"), ("best single model", "sel", "C3"),
                      ("full model", "full", "C2")]:
    ax.plot(bt.index, np.cumsum(bt["lps_" + key] - bt["lps_bench"]), color=col, label=lab)
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", ls=":", lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlabel("forecast origin"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative log score minus prevailing mean")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Thirty-six years of forecasting, and almost nothing to show for it")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for lab, key in [("BMA", "bma"), ("best single", "sel"), ("full", "full")]:
    c = np.cumsum(bt["lps_" + key] - bt["lps_bench"])
    print(f"{lab:12s}: ends at {c.iloc[-1]:+.2f}, ranging from {c.min():+.2f} to {c.max():+.2f}")
```

Nothing beats the prevailing mean by much, and the ranking among the three
alternatives is the chapter's main empirical point. The full model ends $0.55$
cumulative log points above the benchmark, BMA ends $0.37$ below it, and selecting the
single most probable model each month ends $3.42$ below it, roughly nine times BMA's
shortfall. Selection is the only one of the three with a visible downward drift over
the whole thirty-six years, exactly what R-9.1 predicts when the model space is this
close to indistinguishable: the leading model changes hands repeatedly, carrying a
mean posterior weight of only $0.274$, so a strategy that trusts it fully is
repeatedly betting on whichever specification happened to look best a month or two
earlier.

### The predictive density, and whether it is calibrated

**Reading the computation.** The mixture density at the final forecast origin is
formed by summing thirty-two weighted Student $t$ densities on a grid. The probability
integral transform of a correct predictive CDF, evaluated at the outcome that actually
occurred, should be uniform on $[0,1]$ if the forecast is calibrated.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predictive-and-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Left: the BMA predictive density at the final forecast origin against the prevailing-mean and leading-model densities. Right: probability integral transforms of the BMA density over the 437-month backtest."
t_last = n_p - 1
w_L, _, _, mu_L, sc_L, nu_L = fit_full(np.arange(t_last), Zp[t_last], yp[t_last])
grid_r = np.linspace(-18, 18, 801)
mix = sum(w_L[j] * stats.t.pdf(grid_r, nu_L[j], mu_L[j], sc_L[j]) for j in range(len(models_r)))
j_lead = int(np.argmax(w_L))
var_within = float(w_L @ (sc_L ** 2 * nu_L / (nu_L - 2)))
var_between = float(w_L @ (mu_L - float(w_L @ mu_L)) ** 2)

pit = []
for t in range(t_start, n_p):
    w, _, _, mu, sc, nu = fit_full(np.arange(t), Zp[t], yp[t])
    pit.append(float(w @ stats.t.cdf(yp[t], nu, mu, sc)))
pit = np.array(pit)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
axes[0].plot(grid_r, mix, color="C0", lw=2.0, label="BMA mixture")
axes[0].plot(grid_r, stats.t.pdf(grid_r, nu_L[j_const], mu_L[j_const], sc_L[j_const]),
             color="C7", ls="--", lw=1.4, label="prevailing mean")
axes[0].plot(grid_r, stats.t.pdf(grid_r, nu_L[j_lead], mu_L[j_lead], sc_L[j_lead]),
             color="C3", ls=":", lw=1.2, label=f"leader {labels_r[j_lead]}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("excess return next month (%)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("density")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); axes[0].set_title("The predictive density hardly depends on the model")
axes[1].hist(pit, bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 11), density=True, color="C0", alpha=0.75,
             edgecolor="white")
axes[1].axhline(1.0, color="grey", ls="--")
axes[1].set_xlabel("PIT of the BMA density"); axes[1].set_ylabel("density")
axes[1].set_title("Calibration over the backtest")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"within-model variance {var_within:.2f}, between-model variance {var_between:.4f} "
      f"({100*var_between/(var_within+var_between):.2f}% of the total)")
print(f"PIT: mean {pit.mean():.3f}, share below 0.1 {(pit<0.1).mean():.3f}, "
      f"share above 0.9 {(pit>0.9).mean():.3f}")
```

The three densities in the left panel are visually indistinguishable, standard
deviations near $4.44$ centred within a fifth of a point of each other, and the
variance decomposition explains why: disagreement among the thirty-two models about
next month's mean accounts for only $0.15$ percent of the total predictive variance,
so essentially all of a forecaster's uncertainty about next month's market return is
irreducible, not a question any model in this set claims to resolve. The right panel
is the consolation prize. The probability integral transforms average $0.525$ against
a target of one half, with $9.8$ percent of outcomes below the tenth percentile and
$9.4$ percent above the ninetieth, both close to the nominal ten percent. The model
cannot say where the market is going, but it can say, honestly, how uncertain one
should be about it, which for a risk manager sizing a position is the more valuable of
the two statements.

## Discussion: averaging is insurance, not a discovery procedure {#sec-discussion}

The check against something already known is the shape of the whole exercise, and it
is worth putting a number on the out-of-sample $R^2$ that the log scores above imply,
because that statistic is exactly the one the return-predictability literature reports.

**Reading the computation.** `r2_oos` compares each strategy's squared forecast error
against the prevailing-mean benchmark's, using the same backtest already computed;
zero is the benchmark's own score by construction, and a negative value means the
strategy did worse than always forecasting the historical average.

```{python}
#| label: fig-r2-oos-check
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample R-squared against the prevailing mean, the standard metric of the return-predictability literature, for each strategy over the same 1990-2026 backtest."
r2_bma = r2_oos("mu_bma")
print(f"out-of-sample R2 vs prevailing mean: BMA {r2_bma:.4f}, prevailing mean 0 (by construction)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.0))
ax.bar(["BMA", "prevailing mean"], [r2_bma, 0.0], color=["C0", "C7"])
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("out-of-sample R2 vs prevailing mean")
ax.set_title("Negative out-of-sample R2 is the Goyal-Welch result")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

BMA's out-of-sample $R^2$ against the prevailing mean is $-0.0030$: a forecaster using
all five predictors through the BMA mixture would have produced larger squared errors,
on net, than one who simply projected the historical average return every month. That
is the Goyal and Welch result, that standard return predictors fail to beat the
prevailing mean out of sample, reproduced here with Bayesian machinery on a fresh
sample and a different set of models, and it lands in the same place the literature
has landed for two decades. That agreement is itself evidence
that nothing about this chapter's implementation is an artefact; a method that finds
strong predictability where a large literature has repeatedly failed to would be the
one to distrust.

The comparison among strategies is the result actually worth taking away, and it does
not depend on predictability existing. When the posterior is spread almost evenly
across thirty-two candidates, selecting the leader is close to arbitrary from one
month to the next, and forecasting as though the leader were certainly correct quotes
a density sharper than the evidence supports around a centre chosen by noise, which
R-9.1 already said would happen and the backtest confirms costs nine times what
averaging costs. Averaging is not a way to discover which predictor works. It is
insurance against not knowing, priced correctly, and the price is a small, measured
amount of sharpness given up in exchange for never being the model that was
confidently wrong.

There is a limitation this backtest cannot touch, and it is the reason model
averaging alone is not the end of the course. Every specification compared here is a
static linear regression: parameters that do not move, coefficients that describe the
whole sample the same way regardless of when a predictor is measured relative to when
policy changed. Chapter 10 turns to a setting where that limitation is not about
which of several linear models to trust, but about whether a linear model of any kind
can answer the question at all: the estimated effect of Federal Reserve tightening on
the economy flips sign when the rule used to date policy tightenings changes, and no
amount of averaging over specifications repairs that, because the problem is not model
uncertainty but a causal question that more data, by themselves, cannot settle.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 9 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/09-prediction-bma.qmd) works through them, adds a
worked derivation of the g-prior's dimension penalty and of the log score's
calibration-sharpness decomposition, and revisits a simulated model space where the
true model is known.

1. By hand. Two models are compared on $n$ observations with $R^2_1 < R^2_2$ under the
   g-prior with $g = n$ and $k_2 = k_1 + 1$. Using R-9.3, derive the condition on
   $R^2_2 - R^2_1$ under which the log Bayes factor favours the larger model, and show
   that this threshold shrinks as $n$ grows but never reaches zero.

2. Computational. Refit the backtest of @sec-empirical replacing the g-prior's
   unit-information choice $g = n$ with $g = 4$, a much tighter prior, and report how
   the posterior inclusion probabilities and the out-of-sample ranking of BMA against
   selection change. Explain the direction of the change using R-9.3.

3. On real data. Add the ten-year Treasury yield's own level, rather than the term
   spread, as a sixth candidate predictor, re-enumerate the now $2^6 = 64$ models, and
   report whether the winner's-curse gap of R-9.1, estimated as in @sec-problem,
   grows with the larger model space as the derivation predicts it should.

Exercise 1 is worth attempting before the session, since the dimension penalty it asks
for is used without derivation in the session's own material. Exercises 2 and 3 reuse
the code of @sec-empirical with the prior or the predictor set changed.

## Reading and references

The predictive distribution of R-9.2 and the marginal likelihood of R-9.3 follow UPM
Classes 1 and 5. Madigan and Raftery (1994) is the source for treating the model index
itself as an unknown with a posterior, and for Occam's window, keeping only models
whose odds against the leader clear a threshold, which becomes necessary once
enumeration is no longer feasible. Hoeting, Madigan, Raftery and Volinsky (1999) is the
standard tutorial reference. The log predictive score and its calibration-sharpness
decomposition are due to Gneiting and Raftery (2007). Goyal and Welch's finding that
standard predictors fail to beat the prevailing mean out of sample is the empirical
benchmark @sec-empirical reproduces. The data are the FRED macroeconomic and
Fama-French factor files distributed with this course as repository snapshots.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Madigan and Raftery (1994), "Model Selection and Accounting for Model Uncertainty in
Graphical Models Using Occam's Window," *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*. Hoeting, Madigan, Raftery, and Volinsky (1999), "Bayesian Model
Averaging: A Tutorial," *Statistical Science*. Gneiting and Raftery (2007), "Strictly
Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation," *Journal of the American
Statistical Association*. Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 2-4 and 11. Chan, Koop,
Poirier, and Tobias, *Bayesian Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. 2.
